newsitem.title: UK: Peace in N. Ireland priority for Blair.
newsitem.headline: Peace in N. Ireland priority for Blair.

text.p: British Labour leader Tony Blair promised on Thursday that he would try as hard as Prime Minister John Major to bring peace to Northern Ireland if he wins power.

"I will make this every bit as much a priority for myself as it has been for Mr Major when he's been prime minister," Blair, hot favourite to win the May 1 election, said in a television interview from Glasgow.
"I really believe it is a one-off opportunity that we have for this generation to build peace in Northern Ireland and we don't want to squander that," he told Channel Four television.

Labour's Northern Ireland spokesman, Mo Mowlem, caused controversy at the weekend when she suggested that Sinn Fein, the political wing of the IRA, should be invited to talks on the province's future, due to resume on June 3, if the guerrillas laid down their arms.

Ministers and leaders of Northern Ireland's pro-British Protestant majority accused her of naivety at best and, at worst, favouring nationalists who want Britain to quit the province so it can be reunited with the Irish Republic.
Major blamed the IRA for planting a bomb on one of Britain's major motorways on Thursday that caused traffic chaos. Last week the IRA admitted bombing an important rail junction.
The section on Northern Ireland in Labour's election manifesto, released earlier on Thursday, was short on detail.

It said there was general acceptance of the principle that the future of the province must be determined by the consent of the people, as set out in the 1993 Anglo-Irish blueprint for ending nearly three decades of guerrilla conflict.

But Labour recognised that the option of a united Ireland did not command the consent of Protestant Unionists, who want to preserve the union with Britain, while the province's current British status did not command the consent of Catholic nationalists.
"We are therefore committed to reconciliation between the two traditions and to a new political settlement which can command the support of both," the manifesto said.
It said Labour would help build trust and confidence by acting to guarantee human rights, strengthen confidence in policing, combat discrimination at work and reduce tensions over sectarian parades.
Blair said he hoped the bipartisan approach to Northern Ireland would continue if Labour, out of power since 1979, won the election.
Blair, who earlier met shoppers in the marginal seat of Stirling held by Scottish Secretary Michael Forsyth, was in Glasgow for Friday's launch of Labour's Scottish manifesto.
Opinion polls show he is on course to sweep to power but he said he was taking nothing for granted.
"I carry on working for every piece of support and every bit of trust we can from now until polling day. That's the way we've operated for the past three years.
"It's the way we'll operate for the next four weeks and then in government we'll repay that trust by governing well and sensibly in accordance with the manifesto we've published," he said.
